1142.title: The breath and the Name
1142.hook: the yogis speak of breath practice; Nanak points to the Name within the breath
1142.howItsDone: Sikhs practice simran by repeating the Name, often Waheguru, and some match it to the breath, silently or aloud; the Sukhmani, with its call to remember with every breath, is recited in homes and gurdwaras.

segments.voice: Yesterday, in the Sidh Gosht, Nanak told the yogis that no one finds the way alone. Your line was a guide is needed.

A breath went in just now. Nobody asked it to. Another will come, and another, all day, through meetings and traffic and sleep, without a single instruction from you. The yogis who sit across from Guru Nanak in the Sidh Gosht had made a whole discipline of that quiet traffic: how to hold the breath, slow it, steer it, master it. They bring it up, and Nanak doesn't wave it away. He answers. But he points somewhere they might not expect.
screen: `A BREATH, WITHOUT INSTRUCTIONS.` → `THE YOGIS: MASTER THE BREATH.` → `NANAK POINTS ELSEWHERE.`

segments.voice: Start with what the yogis brought to the mountain. In the dialogue, theirs is a path of discipline: postures, earrings, the patched coat, and work with the breath. The breath was something to train. Nanak's answers, all through the Sidh Gosht, keep coming back to the Word, the Shabad, held inside. So when talk turns to the breath, the poem doesn't tell anyone to stop. Read beside the rest of his answers, the question shifts: not how long the breath is held, but what it carries. That idea runs all through the Guru Granth Sahib. Guru Arjan, in the Sukhmani, puts it in a phrase Sikhs still use: saas saas simrahu Gobind. In paraphrase: remember the Lord with every breath, and the worry inside the mind lifts. Notice the shape of that. Not one great breath held for a long time. Every breath, the ordinary ones: the one at the red light, the one in your sleep. The word for this remembering is simran, and some Sikhs do it by letting the Name, Waheguru, ride the breath in and out, quietly, without forcing anything. So here's the turn. For the yogis, the breath was a thing to conquer. In this reading, it becomes a carrier, and what it carries matters more than how long you can hold it. Nothing here asks anyone to give up a breathing exercise. The Guru's point, as tradition reads it, is that the breath was never the goal. The Name inside it was.
screen: `THE YOGIS TRAINED THE BREATH.` · `NANAK ASKS WHAT IT CARRIES.` · `SAAS SAAS: WITH EVERY BREATH.` · `SIMRAN RIDES THE ORDINARY BREATH.` · then, large: `THE NAME IN THE BREATH.`

segments.voice: Don't change your breathing at all; just let ten breaths come. If you'd like, let Waheguru ride each one, wahe on the way in, guru on the way out, or use a word that matters to you, or simply count, and if you lose count, start again without scolding yourself. When the ten are done, keep sitting, and notice that the breath keeps going without you.
The breath and the Name. In the Sidh Gosht, the yogis train the breath; Nanak points to what it carries. Guru Arjan's phrase: remember with every breath. Today's word.
screen: `THE BREATH AND THE NAME — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the name in the breath. Every ordinary breath can carry it. See you tomorrow.

1143.title: The true yogi
1143.hook: a true yogi is one who lives the Guru's teaching in ordinary life
1143.howItsDone: Sikh teaching honors the householder's life: Sikhs are encouraged to work, raise families and serve others while keeping the Name, rather than leaving home for the forest.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the yogis trained the breath, and Nanak pointed to what it carries. Your line was the name in the breath.

What does a yogi look like? Ask around and the answers come quickly. Someone thin, cross-legged on a mountain, far from phones and rent. Ash on the skin, maybe. Big earrings. A staff. Silence. The Siddhs in the Sidh Gosht looked something like that, and they had paid for it: they had left homes and families to live apart. Across from them sits Nanak, who, tradition says, went home to a family and fields. So a question hangs over the whole conversation: where is yoga found?
screen: `A MOUNTAIN, ASH, A STAFF.` → `THE SIDDHS LEFT HOME.` → `WHERE IS YOGA FOUND?`

segments.voice: In the Sidh Gosht, Nanak's answer keeps returning to one figure: the Gurmukh, the person turned toward the Guru. It is the Gurmukh who finds the way of yoga, through the Word. The old phrase for it is jog jugat, the method of yoga. Nanak doesn't throw the phrase out. He fills it with something else. A short hymn of his in Raga Suhi sits beside the Sidh Gosht like a summary. In paraphrase: yoga is not the patched coat, not the staff, not ash rubbed on the body. It isn't earrings or a shaved head or the blowing of a horn. Then the line that turns it: stay spotless in the middle of the soot. That is how the way of yoga is found. Soot. That's the picture. Not a clean mountain far away, but the smoky kitchen, the office, the crowded bus, the family argument. The test isn't whether you can stay pure where nothing touches you. It's whether you can stay clear where everything does. That's why Sikh teaching honors the householder: someone who earns a living, cooks, cares for the young and the old, and keeps the Name through all of it. The yogis' discipline was real, and Nanak doesn't call them lazy. He moves the discipline indoors, into the hours most people already live. A true yogi, in this reading, might be wiping a counter right now, or waiting in a slow checkout line, steady. The coat and the staff aren't the point. The way you do the next ordinary thing is.
screen: `THE GURMUKH FINDS THE WAY.` · `NOT THE COAT, NOT THE STAFF.` · `SPOTLESS IN THE MIDDLE OF THE SOOT.` · `THE DISCIPLINE MOVES INDOORS.` · then, large: `YOGA IN DAILY LIFE.`

segments.voice: Pick one ordinary thing close by, a cup to wash, a shirt to fold, a plant to water, and give it your whole attention, its weight, its temperature, its sound, the way the yogis gave theirs to the breath. When your mind runs ahead to the next job, bring it back to this one. If you pray, keep the Name in mind while your hands work; if you don't, the full attention is enough.
The true yogi. In Nanak's answer, the Gurmukh, who keeps the Word in ordinary life and stays spotless in the middle of the soot. Today's word.
Your line: yoga in daily life. The soot is where the way is found. That's the mountain for today.

1144.title: Humble before truth
1144.hook: the dialogue ends with the yogis honoring the Word
1144.howItsDone: Sikhs bow before the Guru Granth Sahib on entering a gurdwara, touching the forehead to the floor, and the Asa di Var, with its verse on sweetness and humility, is sung in gurdwaras in the early morning.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the true yogi: spotless in the middle of the soot. Your line was yoga in daily life.

An old balance scale: two pans hanging from a beam. Put something on each side and watch. One pan rises, the other sinks, and the one that sinks has more in it. Guru Nanak used that scale. The Siddhs in the Sidh Gosht were people of standing, masters of hard disciplines, used to being the ones others came to. The dialogue is long, and the questions are sharp. So how does a meeting like that end, between people who don't bend easily?
screen: `TWO PANS ON A BEAM.` → `THE HEAVIER ONE SINKS.` → `THE YOGIS BOWED.`

segments.voice: First, the ending. It's told in more than one place. The Sidh Gosht itself closes on the Word: in paraphrase, without the True Word there is no freedom, and the Gurmukh is the one who finds it. Bhai Gurdas, the early Sikh poet whose Vaars are read alongside scripture, tells of Nanak meeting the Siddhs, and in his telling they end by praising the work of Nanak's life, a life spent pointing to the Name. Read together, the honor doesn't land on a debating score. It lands on the truth being talked about, and on a life that lived it. Now the scale. In the Asa di Var, Guru Nanak has a short verse about bowing. In paraphrase: everyone bows to themselves; no one bows to another. Put things on a balance and weigh them: the side that bows is the heavier one. We usually think the one who stays upright is strong and the one who bends is weak. The verse turns it over. Bowing shows weight; the empty pan floats up. Right beside that verse, the Asa di Var gives two words that sum it up, mithat neevee: sweetness and humility, the essence of virtue and goodness. So when the yogis bow, it isn't a defeat on a scoreboard. Masters of their craft, they still had room to honor something true from outside their own order. That's heavy. And at the start of the dialogue, before a single argument, Nanak's first move was a bow to the True One. Humility runs both ways across that mountain.
screen: `THE HONOR GOES TO THE WORD.` · `THE SIDE THAT BOWS IS HEAVIER.` · `SWEETNESS AND HUMILITY.` · `HUMILITY RUNS BOTH WAYS.` · then, large: `THE YOGIS BOWED.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who once told you something true you didn't want to hear: a coach who corrected you, a friend who disagreed, maybe someone younger than you. Remember what they said and how long it took you to see it, then lower your head a little, not to make yourself small, just to give the weight its due. If you pray, give thanks for them; if you don't, hold them in mind with gratitude.
Humble before truth. The yogis honor the Word, not the winner; and in Guru Nanak's scale, the side that bows is the heavier one. Today's word.
Your line: the yogis bowed. Sweetness and humility, mithat neevee, travel together. Rest well.

1145.title: Dialogue, not debate
1145.hook: Nanak listens and answers; he does not mock
1145.howItsDone: Sikh teaching values sweet speech, and the Sidh Gosht is read as a model of conversation with other seekers; it is recited in full in some Sikh homes and gurdwaras.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the yogis bowed, and in Nanak's scale the side that bows is the heavier one. Your line was the yogis bowed.

A reply is half typed. The other person said something wrong, maybe a little smug, and the perfect line is ready, the kind that would get laughs. The thumb hovers over send. The Sidh Gosht has a moment like that. The yogis come at Nanak with hard questions, some of them pointed: who are you, where do you come from, why did you leave home. He had every chance to score points.
screen: `A REPLY, HALF TYPED.` → `THE PERFECT CUTTING LINE.` → `HARD QUESTIONS ON THE MOUNTAIN.`

segments.voice: Look first at the shape of the thing. Sidh Gosht means the discourse with the Siddhs, and it's written that way: they ask, he answers, question after question. It isn't a speech to an audience. It's a conversation with people in it. Now look at how he answers. Over the past days we've met their words: earrings, the patched coat, the breath, the way of yoga. Nanak never throws those words back at them. He picks each one up, turns it in the light, and fills it with something new. True earrings, he says: the Guru's Word. The way of yoga: the Word lived in ordinary life. That takes the other person's language seriously enough to use it. Mockery does the opposite: it holds someone's words up to be laughed at. Guru Nanak has a short verse about this in the Asa di Var. In paraphrase: speak harsh, tasteless words, and body and mind turn harsh and tasteless too. The word he uses is phikka, flat, without savor, like food with no salt. A cutting reply might win the room, but in that verse it leaves the speaker poorer. A disagreement often offers the same fork: debate, where someone has to lose, or dialogue, where both people leave having been heard. The Sidh Gosht doesn't pretend the yogis and Nanak agreed on everything. It shows that strong disagreement and kindness can sit in the same circle.
screen: `THEY ASK, HE ANSWERS.` · `HE USES THEIR OWN WORDS.` · `PHIKKA: HARSH, WITHOUT SAVOR.` · `DISAGREE, AND STAY KIND.` · then, large: `ANSWER KINDLY.`

segments.voice: Bring back a question someone asked you recently that annoyed you, notice the quick, sharp answer that rises first, and let it pass. Then look for the kind answer, honest and still your own view, but spoken so the other person could take it in, and rehearse it once. If you pray, ask for sweet speech; if not, simply let the sharp answer go.
Dialogue. The Sidh Gosht is built as a conversation: the yogis ask, Nanak answers, and he never mocks. Today's word.
Your line: answer kindly. Their own words, with salt, not bite. Until tomorrow.

1146.title: Sidh Gosht close
1146.hook: a conversation with other seekers, still worth having
1146.howItsDone: The Sidh Gosht is in Raga Ramkali in the Guru Granth Sahib; Sikhs read it in the course of a full reading of the scripture, and kirtan singers sing stanzas from it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, dialogue: Nanak used the yogis' own words and never mocked them. Your line was answer kindly.

Most conversations vanish. Somebody says goodnight, the porch light goes off, and whatever was said lives on only in the two people who were there. A few get written down. Fewer still get sung. The talk between Guru Nanak and the Siddhs on the mountain did not vanish. It sits in the Guru Granth Sahib, in Raga Ramkali, and Sikhs still read it and sing it: a conversation between seekers who did not agree, kept as scripture. For two weeks we've sat in that circle. Today we stand and look back at it.
screen: `MOST CONVERSATIONS VANISH.` → `THIS ONE BECAME SCRIPTURE.` → `LOOKING BACK AT THE CIRCLE.`

segments.voice: Walk around the circle once. It began with a question as old as strangers: who are you, where do you come from. Asked how to live, Nanak gave the lotus and the duck: in the water, not soaked by it. Asked why he left home, he said: to seek the Gurmukhs, the people turned toward the Guru. The yogis' earrings became the Guru's Word. Asked where it all began, he spoke of wonder. Asked where the mind lives, he said the Word steadies it. Then the answer some readers call the center of the whole dialogue: the Word is the Guru, and attention tuned to it is the disciple. The world as an ocean, the Word as the boat. A guide is needed. The breath carries the Name. The true yogi is spotless in the middle of the soot. And, read beside a verse from the Asa di Var, the side that bows is the heavier one. Notice what held all that together. Not agreement. The yogis never stopped being yogis, as far as the text tells us. What held it was that both sides kept talking: real questions, real answers, in the other side's own language. That may be the quietest teaching of the Sidh Gosht: a conversation with other seekers is worth having all the way through. Sikhs keep it in scripture, beside the Gurus' hymns of praise. Talking honestly with people on a different path can be part of the path itself.
screen: `WHO ARE YOU? THE DUCK STAYS DRY.` · `THE WORD IS THE GURU.` · `NOT AGREEMENT: THEY KEPT TALKING.` · `CONVERSATION AS PART OF THE PATH.` · then, large: `KEEP TALKING.`

segments.voice: Think of someone you'd like to really talk with, a friend who sees things differently, a parent, a neighbor whose faith isn't yours, and choose one real question the yogis might have asked: where do you come from, what steadies you, what's it all for. Then imagine listening to the whole answer without planning your reply. If you pray, ask for an open ear; if not, simply hold the person in mind.
Sidh Gosht close. The end of the dialogue with the yogis: two paths that didn't agree, a conversation that held, and scripture that kept it. Today's word.
Your line: keep talking. A real question deserves the whole answer. Two weeks on the mountain, done.

1147.title: An alphabet of wisdom
1147.hook: tradition sets it at Onkareshwar, where Nanak answered a pandit with a poem on the letters
1147.howItsDone: The Oankar, Guru Nanak's poem on the letters, is in Raga Ramkali in the Guru Granth Sahib; Sikh children learning Gurmukhi are often taught that the script carries the Guru's Word.

segments.voice: Yesterday we closed the Sidh Gosht: a conversation with other seekers, kept as scripture. Your line was keep talking.

A, apple. B, ball. C, cat. Somewhere a child is chanting letters right now, pointing at a picture for each one. Tradition tells of Guru Nanak coming to Onkareshwar, a temple town on a river, and meeting a pandit there, a learned teacher of scripture and letters. Nanak answered him with a poem that walks through the letters one by one. But the picture hung on each letter isn't an apple or a ball. The poem's name is Oankar.
screen: `A, APPLE. B, BALL.` → `A PANDIT AT ONKARESHWAR.` → `A POEM ON THE LETTERS.`

segments.voice: The poem sits in Raga Ramkali, just before the Sidh Gosht. Its heading calls it Dakhni Oankar, Oankar of the south, which fits the tradition that places it at a temple south of the Punjab. Oankar is a name for the One: the sound at the head of the Guru Granth Sahib itself, in the symbol Ik Oankar, One Creator. So the poem's title is also its subject. Here's how it works. In the story, the pandit is a kind of gatekeeper: learn the letters, and the scriptures open. Nanak keeps the gate and changes what's behind it. A letter is named, and then, instead of a word to spell, comes a teaching about the One, about the mind, about how to live. The alphabet becomes a ladder of wisdom. That isn't an attack on learning. Guru Nanak honored letters. In the Japji he says, in paraphrase: through letters we speak the Name, through letters we praise; through letters come knowledge and song; through letters things are written and spoken. Letters are a gift. The Oankar asks what we do with them: spell our way to arguments, or let each letter point somewhere true. And there's something tender in the form. An alphabet is an ordinary schoolroom thing, learned early. Nanak meets a scholar with the simplest tool in the room and fills it to the brim. Over the next days we'll read pieces of it.
screen: `DAKHNI OANKAR: OANKAR OF THE SOUTH.` · `OANKAR: A NAME FOR THE ONE.` · `THROUGH LETTERS WE PRAISE.` · `EACH LETTER CARRIES WISDOM.` · then, large: `LETTERS OF WISDOM.`

segments.voice: The poem's name begins with the Gurmukhi sound o, written ਓ; look at it for a moment, then close your eyes and trace its shape in the air, slowly, the way a child would, saying the sound softly. If you already read Gurmukhi, choose a letter you love instead, and let it carry one thing you know about the One. If you pray, let the letter become a short prayer of attention; if not, just stay with the shape and the sound.

1148.title: Oankar made all
1148.hook: from the One came Brahma and all creation
1148.howItsDone: The Guru Granth Sahib opens with Ik Oankar, the One Creator; the Oankar in Raga Ramkali opens by tracing all creation back to that One.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Oankar, Guru Nanak's poem on the letters, answered to a pandit. Your line was letters of wisdom.

Pick up the nearest object, a mug, say. Someone shaped it, someone fired it, someone dug the clay. The clay came out of a hillside, and the hillside came out of something older still. Follow any made thing back, and the trail gets long and strange very fast. The Oankar starts at the far end of that trail. Its opening lines don't begin with a letter to learn. They begin with where everything came from.
screen: `A MUG, A POTTER, A HILLSIDE.` → `FOLLOW IT BACK.` → `THE OANKAR STARTS AT THE END.`

segments.voice: Here is the opening of the Oankar, in paraphrase. From Oankar, Brahma came to be. Brahma kept Oankar in his mind. From Oankar came the mountains and the ages. From Oankar the Vedas were made. Remember who Nanak is speaking to, in the tradition: a pandit, a teacher of the Vedas. So the poem opens in the pandit's own world: Brahma, the creator in his own tradition; the Vedas, the scriptures he taught. Nanak dismisses none of them. He traces each back to its source. Brahma came from the One, and remembered the One. The mountains, the long ages, the holy books themselves: from Oankar. It's the move we watched in the Sidh Gosht, using the other person's language, now in a schoolroom instead of on a mountain. And it's the move the mug made a minute ago. Whatever is in front of you, a scripture, a mountain, a cup, follow it back far enough and the poem says you arrive at one place. Notice the word kept in that second line. In the poem, even Brahma, the creator, is a rememberer. That matters for an ordinary day: if everything comes from the One, nothing in front of you is a stranger to it. Look back over this week's lines: the name in the breath, yoga in daily life, the yogis bowed, answer kindly, keep talking, letters of wisdom. And now the root under all of them: from the one.
screen: `FROM OANKAR, BRAHMA.` · `THE MOUNTAINS, THE AGES, THE VEDAS.` · `THE PANDIT'S OWN WORLD, TRACED BACK.` · `NOTHING IS A STRANGER TO IT.` · then, large: `FROM THE ONE.`

segments.voice: Choose something within reach, a cup, a pencil, a slice of bread, and follow it back one slow step at a time: who made it, what it was made of, where that came from, and before that. Don't hurry to an answer at the end; just notice how many hands and how much earth are in one small thing. If you pray, let the trail end in the One the Oankar names; if not, rest in the wonder of the trail itself.
